scenes.label: "THE GLOW"
scenes.script_text: Pick up an iPhone tonight, and you are not holding a telephone.

scenes.label: "THE ARTIFACT"
scenes.script_text: You are holding the most profitable consumer object ever created by the human species.

scenes.label: "PRECISION"
scenes.script_text: A single block of machined titanium, glass, and microscopic silicon.

scenes.label: "THE IPHONE HEAVYWEIGHT"
scenes.script_text: In a single ninety-day quarter, this device generates more profit than Nike, Coca-Cola, and McDonald's combined.
Behind that glass is a company valued at more than three trillion dollars.

scenes.label: "ECONOMIC WEIGHT"
scenes.script_text: That is larger than the entire gross domestic product of the United Kingdom, France, or India.

scenes.label: "LIQUID FORTRESS"
scenes.script_text: Apple's cash reserves could buy entire airline fleets, hotel chains, or defense contractors in cash by lunchtime.

scenes.label: "THE WEB"
scenes.script_text: It commands a global supply chain spanning six continents.

scenes.label: "ONE BILLION POCKETS"
scenes.script_text: Over one billion people carry an Apple device in their front pocket every second of the day.

scenes.label: "THE DAILY TOLL"
scenes.script_text: When an alarm rings in Sydney, a podcast plays in Tokyo, or a credit card taps in London, Apple takes its toll.

scenes.label: "THE CIVIL ENGINE"
scenes.script_text: It has become the default operating system for modern human civilization.

scenes.label: "THE TEMPLE"
scenes.script_text: Yet the entire illusion is designed to look effortless, friendly, and inevitable.

scenes.label: "THE RITUAL"
scenes.script_text: Smooth rounded corners. Minimalist packaging. Silk-wrapped cables. Friendly smiling typography.

scenes.label: "THE MIRROR"
scenes.script_text: That is the trick. Apple does not sell computers. Apple sells identity.

scenes.label: "THINK DIFFERENT"
scenes.script_text: It sells the flattering belief that using their tools makes you a little more creative, a little more rebellious, a little more special than everyone else.

scenes.label: "THE PRESTIGE"
scenes.script_text: It is the greatest magic trick in corporate history.

scenes.label: "THE SPACESHIP (TODAY)"
scenes.script_text: Because fifty years ago, there was no glass spaceship headquarters in Cupertino.

scenes.label: "YEAR ZERO"
scenes.script_text: There was no billion-dollar marketing budget. There were no clean white retail temples.

scenes.label: "11161 CRIST DRIVE"
scenes.script_text: There was only a drafty suburban garage in Los Altos, California, with oil stains on the concrete floor.

scenes.label: "THE OUTSIDERS"
scenes.script_text: Two college dropouts who had barely twenty-five dollars between them.

scenes.label: "THE WIZARD (WOZ)"
scenes.script_text: One was an awkward, quiet engineering genius who just wanted to build neat electronics.

scenes.label: "THE PROPHET (JOBS)"
scenes.script_text: The other was an intense, manipulative, barefoot college dropout who refused to wear shoes and ate only apples.

scenes.label: "CIRCUITS & WILL"
scenes.script_text: Steve Wozniak built the machines. Steve Jobs gave them a soul—and a price tag.

scenes.label: "THE SEED"
scenes.script_text: Neither of them knew that their frantic little garage hobby was about to trigger an industrial earthquake.

scenes.label: "THE RIFT"
scenes.script_text: Nor did they know that the company they created would one day destroy their friendship,

scenes.label: "THE EXILE"
scenes.script_text: drive Jobs into public humiliation and exile,

scenes.label: "THE COMEBACK"
scenes.script_text: and then, against every rule of Wall Street, resurrect him as the most celebrated corporate icon of the modern world.

scenes.label: "BEHIND THE CURTAIN"
scenes.script_text: This is not the sanitized, polished story from the keynote stage. This is the entire history of Apple.

scenes.label: "REWIND: 1975"
scenes.script_text: To understand how the fruit conquered the planet, you have to rewind to 1975.

scenes.label: "THE BEHEMOTHS"
scenes.script_text: Back when computers were not friendly, pocket-sized companions.

scenes.label: "THE PRIESTHOOD"
scenes.script_text: They were terrifying, multi-million-dollar behemoths locked in air-conditioned basements of banks and military commands.

scenes.label: "THE PUNCH CARDS"
scenes.script_text: Run by a priesthood of men in white lab coats who fed them paper punch cards.

scenes.label: "THE SYSTEM"
scenes.script_text: Ordinary people were not allowed to touch them. Ordinary people were supposed to be managed by them.

scenes.label: "WHY WOULD YOU WANT ONE?"
scenes.script_text: The thought of an individual owning a computer in their own house was considered completely ridiculous.

scenes.label: "THE EXPERT"
scenes.script_text: Ken Olsen, the founder of Digital Equipment Corporation, famously declared:

scenes.label: "FAMOUS LAST WORDS"
scenes.script_text: "There is no reason anyone would want a computer in their home."

scenes.label: "THE COUNTER-CULTURE"
scenes.script_text: He was wrong. And a ragtag gang of California misfits was about to prove it.

scenes.label: "HOMEBREW COMPUTER CLUB"
scenes.script_text: In Menlo Park, California, enthusiasts began gathering every two weeks in a concrete garage for the Homebrew Computer Club.

scenes.label: "THE REBELS"
scenes.script_text: They were hobbyists, phone hackers, anti-war activists, and electronics geeks.

scenes.label: "POWER TO THE PEOPLE"
scenes.script_text: Their philosophy was simple: computers should belong to the people, not corporations or the Pentagon.

scenes.label: "THE QUIET GENIUS"
scenes.script_text: Among them sat twenty-four-year-old Steve Wozniak, an engineer at Hewlett-Packard.

scenes.label: "PURE HOBBY"
scenes.script_text: Woz did not care about money, corporate prestige, or conquering industries.

scenes.label: "ELEGANCE"
scenes.script_text: He cared about engineering elegance. How to do with thirty chips what other engineers needed a hundred to do.

scenes.label: "THE BREAKTHROUGH"
scenes.script_text: In late 1975, Woz had an epiphany.

scenes.label: "THE HOOKUP"
scenes.script_text: Why not connect a cheap television set directly to a keyboard and a microprocessor on a single board?

scenes.label: "FIRST STROKES"
scenes.script_text: On a rainy Sunday in his apartment, Woz typed a few keys on a typewriter keyboard.

scenes.label: "IT SPEAKS"
scenes.script_text: And for the first time in human history, the letters appeared immediately on the television screen in front of him.

scenes.label: "THE OLD WAY DIES"
scenes.script_text: No punch cards. No paper printouts. No waiting hours for mainframe batch processing.

scenes.label: "INSTANT RESPONSE"
scenes.script_text: It was instantaneous personal computing.

scenes.label: "THE OPEN HAND"
scenes.script_text: Woz was so proud that he photocopied the schematics and gave them away to his friends at Homebrew for free.

scenes.label: "RAW COBALT"
scenes.script_text: Deep beneath the earth in the Democratic Republic of Congo, children dig for cobalt.

scenes.label: "THE VOYAGE"
scenes.script_text: The mineral travels across oceans to chemical refineries in Asia.

scenes.label: "SEALED POWER"
scenes.script_text: Before it is sealed forever into a microscopic battery that powers your morning alarms.

scenes.label: "COOL GLASS"
scenes.script_text: You never see the mine. You never see the cargo ship. You only feel the cool glass.

scenes.label: "THE DOPAMINE TRIGGER"
scenes.script_text: Every swipe, every haptic tap is engineered by a team of neuroscientists and psychologists in Cupertino.

scenes.label: "MARIMBA CHIME"
scenes.script_text: The notification sound—the gentle marimba chime—is recognized by more people than Beethoven's Fifth Symphony.

scenes.label: "THE BLUE BOX HACKERS"
scenes.script_text: Before Steve and Woz built computers, they were outlaw telephone pirates.

scenes.label: "2600 HERTZ"
scenes.script_text: Woz discovered that toy whistles from Cap'n Crunch cereal boxes emitted a tone at exactly 2600 Hertz.

scenes.label: "FOOLING THE SWITCHES"
scenes.script_text: That exact frequency fooled AT&T's long-distance telephone switches into granting free international calls anywhere on earth.

scenes.label: "CALLING THE POPE"
scenes.script_text: They used it to call the Vatican in Rome, with Woz pretending to be Henry Kissinger asking to speak to the Pope.

scenes.label: "THE REALIZATION"
scenes.script_text: Then twenty-year-old Steve Jobs saw what Wozniak had built.

scenes.label: "NOT AN ENGINEER"
scenes.script_text: Jobs could not design a circuit board to save his life.

scenes.label: "SEEING THE FUTURE"
scenes.script_text: He did not know assembly language. But he understood something infinitely rarer: human desire.

scenes.label: "THE PITCH"
scenes.script_text: Jobs told Wozniak to stop giving the designs away. 'Let's build circuit boards and sell them for fifty bucks.'

scenes.label: "THE DOUBT"
scenes.script_text: Woz asked: 'What if we lose our money?'

scenes.label: "FOR ONCE IN OUR LIVES"
scenes.script_text: Jobs replied: 'At least we'll have our own company. For once in our lives, we'll have a company.'

scenes.label: "SOLD: THE BUS"
scenes.script_text: To raise the seed money, Jobs sold his beloved Volkswagen microbus for a few hundred dollars.

scenes.label: "SOLD: THE CALCULATOR"
scenes.script_text: Wozniak sold his prized Hewlett-Packard 65 scientific calculator for five hundred.

scenes.label: "SEED CAPITAL: $1,300"
scenes.script_text: Combined, they had thirteen hundred dollars. That was the entire capitalization of Apple Computer.

scenes.label: "THE COMMUNE ROAD"
scenes.script_text: The name was chosen on the drive back from an apple orchard commune where Jobs had been pruning Gravenstein trees.

scenes.label: "APPLE COMPUTER?"
scenes.script_text: Jobs suggested 'Apple Computer.' Woz laughed.

scenes.label: "PAGE ONE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs said it sounded fun, spirited, and not intimidating. Plus, it would put them ahead of Atari in the phone book.

scenes.label: "APRIL FOOLS' DAY, 1976"
scenes.script_text: On April 1, 1976—April Fools' Day—Apple was born.

scenes.label: "THE EXIT"
scenes.script_text: Their third partner, Ronald Wayne, got cold feet twelve days later.

scenes.label: "CASHED OUT FOR $800"
scenes.script_text: He sold his ten percent stake back to Jobs and Woz for eight hundred dollars.

scenes.label: "THE $300B REGRET"
scenes.script_text: Today, that ten percent stake would be worth over three hundred billion dollars.

scenes.label: "THE BYTE SHOP"
scenes.script_text: Jobs took their naked circuit board to Paul Terrell, who ran the Byte Shop in Mountain View.

scenes.label: "THE 50-UNIT ORDER"
scenes.script_text: Terrell looked at it and made a shocking offer: he would buy fifty units.

scenes.label: "$25,000 CONTRACT"
scenes.script_text: But only if they were fully assembled, not kit parts. Price: five hundred dollars each.

scenes.label: "THE JACKPOT"
scenes.script_text: Twenty-five thousand dollars. It was more money than either Jobs or Wozniak had ever seen in their lives.

scenes.label: "THE FACTORY IN THE GARAGE"
scenes.script_text: The garage became an assembly line.

scenes.label: "$1 PER BOARD"
scenes.script_text: Jobs's sister was paid one dollar per board to solder chip sockets.

scenes.label: "MISSION COMPLETE"
scenes.script_text: They delivered the fifty boards. The Apple I was an underground hit among hardcore hobbyists.
They priced it at six hundred and sixty-six dollars and sixty-six cents.

scenes.label: "REPEATING DIGITS"
scenes.script_text: Not out of satanic loyalty, but because Woz liked repeating digits.

scenes.label: "NOT GOOD ENOUGH"
scenes.script_text: The Apple I made them fifteen thousand dollars in profit. But Steve Jobs was already disgusted by it.

scenes.label: "RAW WIRES"
scenes.script_text: It was still just an ugly board of wires. It needed a case, a power supply, and a monitor.

scenes.label: "THE CONSUMER"
scenes.script_text: Jobs realized: true revolution wouldn't come from hobbyists who knew how to solder.

scenes.label: "LIKE A TOASTER"
scenes.script_text: It would come from an appliance. A machine that worked straight out of the box, as friendly as a toaster.

scenes.label: "THE MASTERPIECE"
scenes.script_text: Woz sat down and designed his masterpiece: the Apple II.

scenes.label: "COLOR & SOUND"
scenes.script_text: It was a triumph of engineering: color graphics, built-in sound, game paddles, and expansion slots.

scenes.label: "SILENT & SMOOTH"
scenes.script_text: Jobs obsessed over the case. No metal screws visible. No ugly cooling fan—it had to be silent.

scenes.label: "THE EXACT BEIGE"
scenes.script_text: He spent weeks picking the exact warm shade of beige plastic.

scenes.label: "THE ANGEL (MARKKULA)"
scenes.script_text: To fund production, they needed serious capital. Enter Mike Markkula.

scenes.label: "SPOTTING GENIUS"
scenes.script_text: A retired Intel executive who recognized genius when he saw it.

scenes.label: "THE $250K LIFEBLOOD"
scenes.script_text: Markkula secured a two-hundred-and-fifty-thousand-dollar line of credit and became a one-third partner.

scenes.label: "WEST COAST COMPUTER FAIRE"
scenes.script_text: In April 1977, Apple debuted the Apple II at the West Coast Computer Faire.

scenes.label: "FUTURE ARRIVES"
scenes.script_text: While competitors showed ugly metal boxes with exposed wires, Apple arrived like a consumer company from the future.

scenes.label: "THE AVALANCHE"
scenes.script_text: The orders poured in by the thousands.

scenes.label: "VISICALC: THE SPREADSHEET"
scenes.script_text: Then in 1979, two Harvard programmers invented VisiCalc—the world's first electronic spreadsheet.

scenes.label: "THE KILLER APP"
scenes.script_text: Suddenly, business executives weren't buying an Apple II to play games.

scenes.label: "20 SECONDS VS 20 HOURS"
scenes.script_text: They were buying it because it could do in twenty seconds what had previously taken an accountant twenty hours.

scenes.label: "THE ROCKET SHIP"
scenes.script_text: The Apple II became a cash printing press. Revenue exploded from eight million dollars in 1978 to one hundred and seventeen million in 1980.

scenes.label: "DECEMBER 12, 1980: IPO"
scenes.script_text: On December 12, 1980, Apple Computer went public on Wall Street.

scenes.label: "HISTORIC OFFERING"
scenes.script_text: It was the largest public offering since the Ford Motor Company in 1956.

scenes.label: "300 NEW MILLIONAIRES"
scenes.script_text: In an afternoon, three hundred Apple employees became instant millionaires.

scenes.label: "WORTH $256,000,000 AT 25"
scenes.script_text: Steve Jobs, at age twenty-five, was suddenly worth two hundred and fifty-six million dollars.

scenes.label: "TIME MAGAZINE"
scenes.script_text: He was rich, famous, and on the cover of Time magazine.

scenes.label: "THE BOY KING"
scenes.script_text: He had conquered the world before his hair had even begun to thin.

scenes.label: "HUBRIS"
scenes.script_text: And that is when the arrogance took over.

scenes.label: "ROB JANOFF SKETCHES"
scenes.script_text: When Steve Jobs was designing the original Apple logo, he hired art director Rob Janoff.

scenes.label: "NOT A CHERRY"
scenes.script_text: Janoff added a single curved bite out of the side so people wouldn't confuse it with a cherry or a tomato.

scenes.label: "THE RAINBOW LOGO"
scenes.script_text: Jobs added vibrant rainbow stripes across the fruit to celebrate the Apple II's color screen.

scenes.label: "XEROX PARC (DEC 1979)"
scenes.script_text: In December 1979, Jobs made a pilgrimage that changed computer history forever.

scenes.label: "THE PLAYGROUND OF GENIUSES"
scenes.script_text: Xerox was a copier company whose corporate executives had funded a playground of the world's greatest computer scientists.

scenes.label: "THE SECRET VISIT"
scenes.script_text: In exchange for a hundred thousand shares of pre-IPO Apple stock, Xerox agreed to open the kimono.

scenes.label: "THE THREE TREASURES"
scenes.script_text: They showed Jobs three technologies: object-oriented programming, Ethernet networking, and the graphical user interface.

scenes.label: "BLINDED BY THE SCREEN"
scenes.script_text: Jobs was so blinded by the graphical screen with its rolling desktop mouse that he barely paid attention to the other two.

scenes.label: "THE CRUDE MOUSE"
scenes.script_text: He watched a plastic box with a rubber ball underneath move a pointer smoothly across the screen.

scenes.label: "WHY AREN'T YOU USING THIS?"
scenes.script_text: He began jumping up and down in the lab, shouting at the top of his lungs:

scenes.label: "SITTING ON A GOLD MINE"
scenes.script_text: "Why aren't you doing anything with this? This is the greatest thing! You are sitting on a gold mine!"

scenes.label: "BLIND COPIER TYCOONS"
scenes.script_text: Xerox management was obsessed with selling paper copiers. They had no idea what they had invented.

scenes.label: "THE $15 MOUSE CHALLENGE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs ran back to Apple, assembled his hardware team, and ordered them to build a mouse that cost fifteen dollars instead of three hundred.

scenes.label: "THE DEODORANT BALL HACK"
scenes.script_text: Designer Jim Hovey solved it by using a rubber ball from a bottle of roll-on Ban deodorant.

scenes.label: "CALLIGRAPHY AT REED"
scenes.script_text: When Jobs dropped out of Reed College, he had dropped in on a calligraphy class taught by a Trappist monk named Robert Palladino.

scenes.label: "THE BEAUTY OF LETTERS"
scenes.script_text: He learned about serif and sans-serif typefaces, varying spaces between letters, and what makes great typography artistic.

scenes.label: "PROPORTIONAL FONTS"
scenes.script_text: Ten years later, Jobs forced those fonts into the Macintosh: Chicago, Geneva, Venice, and Monaco.

scenes.label: "CONNECTING THE DOTS"
scenes.script_text: "If I had never dropped in on that single course in college," Jobs recalled, "the Mac would have never had multiple typefaces or proportionally spaced fonts."

scenes.label: "INFALLIBLE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs became convinced of his own infallibility.

scenes.label: "THE LISA"
scenes.script_text: He poured tens of millions of dollars into a new computer named the Lisa, after his daughter.

scenes.label: "$10,000 MISTAKE"
scenes.script_text: It was packed with revolutionary Xerox PARC graphical technology, but it cost ten thousand dollars.

scenes.label: "LUXURY SHIPWRECK"
scenes.script_text: Adjusted for inflation, that is nearly thirty thousand dollars for a single desk computer.

scenes.label: "BURIED IN UTAH"
scenes.script_text: It flopped catastrophically. Apple ended up burying thousands of unsold Lisas in a Utah landfill.

scenes.label: "LOCKED OUT"
scenes.script_text: Humiliated, the board kicked Jobs off the Lisa project.

scenes.label: "BANDLEY 3"
scenes.script_text: Furious, Jobs took over a small skunkworks project inside the company: the Macintosh.

scenes.label: "THE PIRATE FLAG"
scenes.script_text: He declared war on the rest of Apple.

scenes.label: "BETTER TO BE A PIRATE"
scenes.script_text: He hoisted a pirate flag over the Macintosh building and announced:

scenes.label: "THE CREW"
scenes.script_text: "It is better to be a pirate than to join the Navy."

scenes.label: "90 HOURS A WEEK"
scenes.script_text: The Macintosh team worked ninety-hour weeks, fueled by fruit smoothies, espresso, and fear of Jobs's blistering tantrums.

scenes.label: "THE REALITY DISTORTION FIELD"
scenes.script_text: Jobs would reduce engineers to tears, screaming that their code was 'crap' or their power supplies were 'too big.'

scenes.label: "STOLEN GENIUS"
scenes.script_text: Then he would return the next morning and claim their best idea was his own.

scenes.label: "THE IMPOSSIBLE"
scenes.script_text: Yet they stayed. Because he pushed them to do work they didn't know they were capable of.

scenes.label: "THE SUPER BOWL MISSION"
scenes.script_text: To launch the Mac, Jobs demanded a commercial unlike anything the world had ever witnessed.

scenes.label: "RIDLEY SCOTT"
scenes.script_text: He hired Ridley Scott, fresh off directing Blade Runner.

scenes.label: "THE ORWELLIAN CROWD"
scenes.script_text: The commercial drew inspiration from George Orwell's novel, 1984.

scenes.label: "BIG BROTHER (IBM)"
scenes.script_text: IBM was cast as Big Brother, an all-powerful titan commanding a brainwashed populace.

scenes.label: "THE RUNNER"
scenes.script_text: Suddenly, an athletic woman in red running shorts sprints into the hall carrying a heavy sledgehammer.

scenes.label: "THE SMASH"
scenes.script_text: She spins around and hurls the hammer straight through the giant screen, exploding it in a blinding flash of white light.

scenes.label: "1984 WILL NOT BE LIKE 1984"
scenes.script_text: The voiceover declared: 'On January 24th, Apple Computer will introduce Macintosh. And you'll see why 1984 won't be like 1984.'

scenes.label: "THE BOARD REJECTS"
scenes.script_text: Apple's board of directors hated it. They thought it was reckless, arrogant, and insulting to IBM.

scenes.label: "WOZ'S CHEQUE"
scenes.script_text: They ordered the agency to sell off the Super Bowl ad time. Jobs refused. Steve Wozniak even offered to pay half the cost himself.

scenes.label: "96 MILLION STUNNED"
scenes.script_text: On Super Bowl Sunday, January 22, 1984, the ad aired to ninety-six million viewers.

scenes.label: "ADVERTISING CHANGED FOREVER"
scenes.script_text: It aired only once on national television. It changed advertising forever.

scenes.label: "FLINT CENTER, JAN 24, 1984"
scenes.script_text: Two days later, Jobs walked onto the stage at Flint Center in Cupertino.

scenes.label: "THE UNVEILING"
scenes.script_text: He wore a double-breasted suit and a polka-dot bow tie.

scenes.label: "THE FLOPPY DISK"
scenes.script_text: He pulled a small rectangular computer out of a canvas carrying bag.

scenes.label: "HELLO"
scenes.script_text: He put a floppy disk in the drive. The screen lit up. The machine spoke in a synthesized voice:

scenes.label: "IT TALKS"
scenes.script_text: "Hello, I am Macintosh. It sure is great to get out of that bag."

scenes.label: "PANDEMONIUM"
scenes.script_text: The auditorium erupted into five minutes of deafening standing ovations. Grown men cried.

scenes.label: "THE GUI IS BORN"
scenes.script_text: It had a mouse. It had desktop icons, windows, trash cans, and proportional fonts.

scenes.label: "THE ANCESTOR"
scenes.script_text: It was the birth of the personal computer interface that every human uses today.

scenes.label: "THE HANGOVER"
scenes.script_text: Then the hangover hit.

scenes.label: "128K OF RAM"
scenes.script_text: The Macintosh was gorgeous, but it was desperately underpowered.

scenes.label: "NO FAN, OVERHEATING"
scenes.script_text: It had only 128 kilobytes of memory. It had no hard drive. It overheated because Jobs refused to install a fan.

scenes.label: "THE DISK SWAP DANCE"
scenes.script_text: Users had to swap floppy disks back and forth thirty times just to copy a single file.

scenes.label: "SALES FREEZE"
scenes.script_text: Sales hit a brick wall. By late 1984, Apple was producing ten thousand Macs a month and selling barely two thousand.

scenes.label: "HEMORRHAGING CASH"
scenes.script_text: The company was hemorrhaging cash.

scenes.label: "CIVIL WAR"
scenes.script_text: Tensions between Jobs and CEO John Sculley erupted into outright war.

scenes.label: "THE PEPSI CHALLENGE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs had recruited Sculley from Pepsi two years earlier with the legendary challenge:

scenes.label: "SUGAR WATER OR DESTINY"
scenes.script_text: "Do you want to sell sugar water for the rest of your life, or do you want to come with me and change the world?"

scenes.label: "THE EXECUTIVE ULTIMATUM"
scenes.script_text: Now Sculley was the one trying to rein in an out-of-control, toxic founder who terrorized employees and missed targets.

scenes.label: "THE COUP ATTEMPT"
scenes.script_text: In May 1985, Jobs plotted a palace coup to remove Sculley while he was on a business trip to China.

scenes.label: "THE CONFRONTATION"
scenes.script_text: An executive tipped Sculley off. Sculley cancelled the trip and confronted Jobs in a brutal boardroom showdown.

scenes.label: "THE VOTE"
scenes.script_text: Sculley polled the board of directors one by one: 'Who do you back? Me, or Steve?'

scenes.label: "STRIPPED OF POWER"
scenes.script_text: Every single board member backed Sculley. Steve Jobs was stripped of all operational authority.

scenes.label: "SIBERIA"
scenes.script_text: He was banished to an empty office across the street called 'Siberia.'

scenes.label: "SEPTEMBER 17, 1985: RESIGNATION"
scenes.script_text: On September 17, 1985, Steve Jobs resigned from Apple.

scenes.label: "ONE LONE SHARE"
scenes.script_text: He sold all of his Apple stock—millions of shares—keeping just one single share so he could still receive the annual report in the mail.

scenes.label: "BROKEN"
scenes.script_text: He was thirty years old. He was a multi-millionaire. And he was utterly broken.

scenes.label: "THE ARTISTS' GUILD"
scenes.script_text: Jobs treated the Macintosh team not like engineers, but like renaissance painters.

scenes.label: "THE CHAMPAGNE TOAST"
scenes.script_text: On February 10, 1982, Jobs gathered the entire Macintosh team for a champagne toast.

scenes.label: "THE SIGNATURE SHEET"
scenes.script_text: He pulled out a large sheet of drafting paper and had every single engineer sign their name with a black pen.

scenes.label: "MOLDED IN PLASTIC"
scenes.script_text: He then had their signatures molded permanently into the inside plastic of every single Macintosh case.

scenes.label: "REAL ARTISTS SIGN THEIR WORK"
scenes.script_text: "Real artists sign their work," Jobs told them. Even though no customer would ever see it unless they cracked the machine open.

scenes.label: "THE HIDDEN BEAUTY"
scenes.script_text: Jobs obsessed over things no ordinary customer would ever consciously notice.

scenes.label: "PAINT THE BACK OF THE FENCE"
scenes.script_text: His father, Paul Jobs, a machinist, had taught him: 'When you build a fence, you paint the back of it just as well as the front.'

scenes.label: "CIRCUITS AS ARCHITECTURE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs applied that ruthless aesthetic standard to the Macintosh's circuit board layout.

scenes.label: "THE PEPSI SAVIOR"
scenes.script_text: When John Sculley arrived from Pepsi, he was treated like a savior by Wall Street.

scenes.label: "THE CONSUMER PACKAGED EXECUTIVE"
scenes.script_text: Sculley was charismatic, polished, and understood mass-market consumer packaged goods.

scenes.label: "THE HONEYMOON"
scenes.script_text: At first, Jobs and Sculley were inseparable. They called each other dynamic soulmates.

scenes.label: "THE PARTNERSHIP"
scenes.script_text: Sculley was the adult in the room who would handle operations, while Jobs remained the creative lightning rod.

scenes.label: "TOXIC COLLISION"
scenes.script_text: But within eighteen months, the relationship turned into toxic poison.

scenes.label: "THE $2,495 PRICING DISPUTE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs blamed Sculley for pricing the Macintosh at twenty-five hundred dollars instead of two thousand, throttling early sales.

scenes.label: "ROTTING INVENTORY"
scenes.script_text: Sculley blamed Jobs for manufacturing machines that sat rotting in warehouses and refusing to compromise with corporate reality.

scenes.label: "THE WILDERNESS"
scenes.script_text: What followed was the wilderness decade.

scenes.label: "DESKTOP PUBLISHING WAVE"
scenes.script_text: For Apple, the late 1980s started smoothly on the momentum of the Macintosh desktop publishing wave.

scenes.label: "THE DESIGN STANDARD"
scenes.script_text: Aldus PageMaker, Adobe fonts, and the LaserWriter made Apple the undisputed king of creative professionals.

scenes.label: "50% MARGINS, ZERO SOUL"
scenes.script_text: Profit margins reached fifty percent. But the company had lost its visionary soul.

scenes.label: "THE SUITS TAKE OVER"
scenes.script_text: Under a succession of professional CEOs—John Sculley, Michael Spindler, Gil Amelio—Apple bloated.

scenes.label: "THE CONFUSION LABYRINTH"
scenes.script_text: They fractured the product line into dozens of confusing, overlapping models: Quadra, Centris, Performa, PowerBook.

scenes.label: "WHAT DO I BUY?"
scenes.script_text: Customers had no idea what to buy. Even Apple's own salespeople could not explain the difference.

scenes.label: "GRAVEYARD OF GADGETS"
scenes.script_text: They burned hundreds of millions on disastrous science projects: the Newton handheld, the Pippin game console, the QuickTake camera.

scenes.label: "THE ARCHITECT (GATES)"
scenes.script_text: Meanwhile, in Redmond, Washington, an old enemy was methodically sharpening his blade.

scenes.label: "WINDOWS 95 FEVER"
scenes.script_text: In August 1995, Microsoft launched Windows 95.

scenes.label: "THE COPYCAT TRIUMPH"
scenes.script_text: It had a desktop, a taskbar, icons, windows, and a trash can. It copied Apple's graphical interface completely.

scenes.label: "90% MONOPOLY"
scenes.script_text: It was not as elegant as the Mac, but it was on ninety percent of all personal computers on earth.

scenes.label: "THE COLLAPSE"
scenes.script_text: Apple's market share collapsed from sixteen percent to under four percent.

scenes.label: "$1 BILLION IN THE RED"
scenes.script_text: The company was hemorrhaging money. In 1996 alone, Apple lost over one billion dollars.

scenes.label: "THE SYSTEM BOMB"
scenes.script_text: Worse, the aging Macintosh operating system was structurally obsolete. It crashed constantly.

scenes.label: "COPLAND DERAILS"
scenes.script_text: Apple tried and failed for six years to build a replacement operating system code-named Copland.

scenes.label: "90 DAYS TO EXTINCTION"
scenes.script_text: By late 1996, Apple was ninety days from formal bankruptcy.

scenes.label: "MICHAEL DELL'S ADVICE"
scenes.script_text: Michael Dell was publicly asked what he would do if he ran Apple. His response was brutal:

scenes.label: "SHUT IT DOWN"
scenes.script_text: "What would I do? I'd shut it down and give the money back to the shareholders."

scenes.label: "THE EXILE'S LAB"
scenes.script_text: Meanwhile, what had Steve Jobs been doing during his eleven years in exile?

scenes.label: "THE NeXT CUBE"
scenes.script_text: He had founded NeXT Computer, building a breathtaking, magnesium-cased workstation running a revolutionary Unix operating system.

scenes.label: "WHERE THE WEB WAS BORN"
scenes.script_text: It was a commercial failure because it cost ten thousand dollars. But the software was brilliant.

scenes.label: "PIXAR"
scenes.script_text: And Jobs had bought a tiny computer graphics division from George Lucas for five million dollars: Pixar.

scenes.label: "$50M OF HIS OWN MONEY"
scenes.script_text: For nearly a decade, Jobs kept Pixar alive out of his own pocket, burning fifty million dollars of his personal fortune.

scenes.label: "TOY STORY: 1995"
scenes.script_text: Then in November 1995, Pixar released Toy Story—the first feature-length computer-animated film in history.

scenes.label: "BILLIONAIRE PRODIGY"
scenes.script_text: It was a global sensation. When Pixar went public a week later, Steve Jobs's eighty percent stake became worth over one billion dollars.

scenes.label: "THE MATURE TITAN"
scenes.script_text: He had grown up. He was no longer the petulant twenty-five-year-old who threw tantrums in garages.

scenes.label: "SEASONED WILL"
scenes.script_text: He was a seasoned CEO who understood corporate governance, storytelling, and patient long-term execution.

scenes.label: "DECEMBER 1996: THE BUYOUT"
scenes.script_text: In December 1996, desperate for a new operating system, Apple CEO Gil Amelio made a fateful decision.

scenes.label: "THE $429M TROJAN HORSE"
scenes.script_text: Apple bought NeXT for four hundred and twenty-nine million dollars in cash and stock.

scenes.label: "THE RETURN TO INFINITE LOOP"
scenes.script_text: Steve Jobs walked back through the front doors of 1 Infinite Loop as an 'informal advisor.'

scenes.label: "THE TROJAN HORSE"
scenes.script_text: It was the greatest Trojan horse in corporate history. The exile had come home.

scenes.label: "PAUL RAND (1986)"
scenes.script_text: When Jobs founded NeXT in late 1985, he hired legendary graphic designer Paul Rand.

scenes.label: "THE MASTER OF LOGOS"
scenes.script_text: Rand had designed the corporate logos for IBM, UPS, ABC, and Westinghouse. He was seventy-one years old.

scenes.label: "THE BRUTAL DESIGNER"
scenes.script_text: Jobs asked Rand to give him a few options to choose from. Rand replied bluntly:

scenes.label: "$100,000 OR NOTHING"
scenes.script_text: "No. I will solve your problem, and you will pay me one hundred thousand dollars. You don't have to use it. But you will pay me."

scenes.label: "THE NeXT CUBE LOGO"
scenes.script_text: Jobs paid the money. Rand delivered a single design: a tilted black cube with four letters: 'NeXT'. Jobs loved it.

scenes.label: "PERFECT 90-DEGREE ANGLES"
scenes.script_text: Jobs spent millions perfecting the magnesium casing of the NeXT computer, insisting on perfect 90-degree internal right angles.

scenes.label: "DECADE AHEAD"
scenes.script_text: The computer was too expensive for universities, but its software layer—NeXTSTEP—was decades ahead of its time.

scenes.label: "OBJECTIVE-C"
scenes.script_text: It was built on an object-oriented language called Objective-C.

scenes.label: "THE HIDDEN FOUNDATION"
scenes.script_text: Years later, that exact software framework would become the foundation of macOS, iOS, the App Store, and the iPhone.

scenes.label: "JOHN LASSETER"
scenes.script_text: Meanwhile at Pixar, an animator named John Lasseter was experimenting with emotional storytelling using digital algorithms.

scenes.label: "LUXO JR. (1986)"
scenes.script_text: In 1986, they produced Luxo Jr.—a two-minute short film about an adorable bouncing desk lamp.

scenes.label: "SOUL IN SILICON"
scenes.script_text: Audiences at computer graphics conferences were moved to tears by a digital lamp.

scenes.label: "THE INTERSECTION"
scenes.script_text: Jobs realized: technology alone was cold. But technology married with liberal arts could touch the human soul.

scenes.label: "DECAY IN CUPERTINO"
scenes.script_text: Back in Cupertino, Apple was decaying from the inside out.

scenes.label: "THE EMBARRASSING KEYNOTES"
scenes.script_text: CEO Gil Amelio held bizarre, rambling keynote speeches that embarrassed shareholders and exhausted employees.

scenes.label: "THE PURGE"
scenes.script_text: Within seven months, Jobs orchestrated a boardroom purge.

scenes.label: "THE $1 SALARY"
scenes.script_text: Gil Amelio was fired. The board was overhauled. Jobs became interim CEO—the 'iCEO'—taking a salary of one dollar a year.

scenes.label: "MACWORLD BOSTON 1997"
scenes.script_text: In August 1997, Jobs walked onto the stage at Macworld Boston. The company was on the brink of death.

scenes.label: "BILL GATES ON THE SCREEN"
scenes.script_text: He announced a shocking partnership: an old nemesis was bailing them out.

scenes.label: "THE $150M TRUCE"
scenes.script_text: Microsoft invested one hundred and fifty million dollars in non-voting Apple stock and guaranteed Office on Mac for five years.

scenes.label: "THE BOOS"
scenes.script_text: The audience booed. Jobs stopped them cold with a line of devastating pragmatism:

scenes.label: "A NEW DOCTRINE"
scenes.script_text: "We have to let go of this notion that for Apple to win, Microsoft has to lose. For Apple to win, Apple has to do a really good job."

scenes.label: "THE CLEAN SWEEP"
scenes.script_text: Then he took a black marker and marched into the product development room.

scenes.label: "THE 2x2 MATRIX"
scenes.script_text: He drew a simple two-by-two grid on the whiteboard.

scenes.label: "CANCEL THE REST"
scenes.script_text: "Here is what we need: four great products. Two for professionals, two for consumers. Everything else, we cancel."

scenes.label: "SURGICAL FOCUS"
scenes.script_text: He eliminated seventy percent of Apple's product line overnight. Three thousand employees were laid off.

scenes.label: "MEETING JONY IVE"
scenes.script_text: He walked into Apple's design studio and found a young, soft-spoken British designer named Jony Ive.

scenes.label: "THE DUO"
scenes.script_text: Jobs recognized an artistic soulmate. Together, they began redesigning the future.

scenes.label: "THE iMAC G3: BONDI BLUE"
scenes.script_text: In May 1998, Jobs unveiled the machine that saved Apple: the iMac G3.

scenes.label: "TRANSLUCENT & FRIENDLY"
scenes.script_text: It was translucent Bondi blue. It had a handle on top. It threw away the floppy drive and embraced USB.

scenes.label: "FIVE FLAVORS"
scenes.script_text: PC makers laughed. But the iMac became the fastest-selling computer in Apple's history.

scenes.label: "BACK FROM THE DEAD"
scenes.script_text: Apple turned an eighty-seven-million-dollar profit in its first full year under Jobs's return.

scenes.label: "THE DIGITAL HUB"
scenes.script_text: Then came the defining shift: the digital hub strategy.

scenes.label: "THE DIGITAL LIFESTYLE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs realized the personal computer was no longer just for word processing. It was the command center for a digital lifestyle.

scenes.label: "OCTOBER 23, 2001"
scenes.script_text: In October 2001, six weeks after 9/11, Jobs held a low-key press conference in Cupertino.

scenes.label: "THE FIRST iPOD"
scenes.script_text: He reached into his pocket and pulled out a sleek stainless-steel device the size of a deck of cards: the iPod.

scenes.label: "1,000 SONGS IN YOUR POCKET"
scenes.script_text: His pitch was an absolute masterpiece of copywriting: 'One thousand songs in your pocket.'

scenes.label: "IT CANNOT BE SMALLER"
scenes.script_text: During development, an engineer insisted the prototype was as compact as physically possible.

scenes.label: "THE AQUARIUM TEST"
scenes.script_text: Jobs walked over to an office aquarium and dropped the iPod into the water.

scenes.label: "THOSE ARE AIR BUBBLES"
scenes.script_text: As it sank, bubbles floated to the surface. Jobs said: 'Those are air bubbles. That means there's empty space. Make it smaller.'

scenes.label: "THE SILHOUETTES"
scenes.script_text: The iPod conquered the music industry.

scenes.label: "99 CENTS A TRACK"
scenes.script_text: In 2003, Apple launched the iTunes Music Store, selling songs for ninety-nine cents.

scenes.label: "THE MUSIC INDUSTRY SURRENDERS"
scenes.script_text: The record labels, terrified of Napster and internet piracy, surrendered their catalog to Steve Jobs.

scenes.label: "THE WHITE CORDS"
scenes.script_text: Apple was no longer a computer company. It was a digital culture company.

scenes.label: "400 MILLION SOLD"
scenes.script_text: Over four hundred million iPods were sold. But Jobs wasn't satisfied.

scenes.label: "THE HORRIBLE PHONES"
scenes.script_text: He looked at mobile cellphones and saw clunky, hideous plastic bricks covered in tiny plastic buttons.

scenes.label: "EVERYONE HATES THEIR PHONE"
scenes.script_text: He hated every single one of them. 'Everyone hates their phone,' he told his executive team.

scenes.label: "CANNIBALIZATION THREAT"
scenes.script_text: He also realized something terrifying: if cellphones learned to play MP3s, the iPod would die.

scenes.label: "CANNIBALIZE YOURSELF"
scenes.script_text: "If we don't cannibalize ourselves," Jobs warned, "someone else will."

scenes.label: "PROJECT PURPLE"
scenes.script_text: For two secret years, Apple's finest hardware and software engineers labored in lockdown mode on Project Purple.

scenes.label: "PINCH TO ZOOM"
scenes.script_text: They invented multi-touch technology: the ability to swipe, pinch, and zoom on a sheet of pure glass with human fingertips.

scenes.label: "MOSCONE CENTER: JAN 9, 2007"
scenes.script_text: On January 9, 2007, Steve Jobs took the stage at Macworld San Francisco.

scenes.label: "THE PINNACLE"
scenes.script_text: It was the greatest product introduction in the history of business.

scenes.label: "CHANGES EVERYTHING"
scenes.script_text: "Every once in a while, a revolutionary product comes along that changes everything," Jobs began.

scenes.label: "THREE PRODUCTS"
scenes.script_text: "Today, we are introducing three revolutionary products of this class."

scenes.label: "IPOD... PHONE... INTERNET..."
scenes.script_text: "The first one is a widescreen iPod with touch controls. The second is a revolutionary mobile phone."

scenes.label: "ARE YOU GETTING IT?"
scenes.script_text: "And the third is a breakthrough internet communications device."

scenes.label: "ONE DEVICE"
scenes.script_text: "An iPod. A phone. And an internet communicator. Are you getting it? These are not three separate devices."

scenes.label: "iPHONE"
scenes.script_text: "This is one device. And we are calling it: iPhone."

scenes.label: "SWEATING BEHIND THE CURTAIN"
scenes.script_text: The demo was a technological tightrope walk. The phone barely worked.

scenes.label: "THE GOLDEN PATH"
scenes.script_text: The operating system had memory leaks. If Jobs clicked icons in the wrong order, the phone would crash completely.

scenes.label: "ROTATION MAGIC"
scenes.script_text: Jobs performed the forty-five-minute demonstration with absolute flawless perfection. Not a single glitch occurred.

scenes.label: "THE EARTHQUAKE"
scenes.script_text: When Steve Jobs stepped off that stage, the entire mobile industry had been rendered obsolete in forty-five minutes.

scenes.label: "BLACKBERRY'S FATAL SNEER"
scenes.script_text: The CEO of BlackBerry dismissed it, saying enterprise customers would never buy a phone without a physical keyboard.

scenes.label: "BALLMER'S LAUGH"
scenes.script_text: Steve Ballmer, CEO of Microsoft, literally laughed out loud on national television:

scenes.label: "$500 LAUGH"
scenes.script_text: "Five hundred dollars fully subsidized? It is the most expensive phone in the world, and it doesn't appeal to business customers!"

scenes.label: "THE FALLEN GIANTS"
scenes.script_text: Within five years, BlackBerry was virtually wiped off the map. Nokia's mobile business was incinerated.

scenes.label: "THE SUMMIT"
scenes.script_text: And Apple became the most valuable technology company on the face of the earth.

scenes.label: "THE APP STORE: 2008"
scenes.script_text: In 2008, Apple launched the App Store with just five hundred apps.

scenes.label: "THE ECOSYSTEM TREE"
scenes.script_text: It unlocked an entirely new global digital economy: Uber, Instagram, WhatsApp, Airbnb, DoorDash.

scenes.label: "THE 30% TOLL"
scenes.script_text: Apple took thirty percent of every transaction. It was a digital toll road on human culture.

scenes.label: "THE UNSTOPPABLE RUN"
scenes.script_text: Then came the iPad in 2010. The MacBooks with unibody aluminum. The custom silicon chips.

scenes.label: "NO COMPUTERS SHOWN"
scenes.script_text: When Jobs returned to Apple in 1997, his first television commercial was not about computers at all.

scenes.label: "THE MISFITS"
scenes.script_text: It was a sixty-second tribute to the troublemakers and the misfits.

scenes.label: "ROUND PEGS IN SQUARE HOLES"
scenes.script_text: "Here's to the crazy ones," the narration began. "The misfits. The rebels. The troublemakers. The round pegs in the square holes."

scenes.label: "THOSE WHO DO"
scenes.script_text: "Because the people who are crazy enough to think they can change the world... are the ones who do."

scenes.label: "THE RE-ENCHANTMENT"
scenes.script_text: It didn't sell megahertz or gigabytes. It re-established Apple as the brand for dreamers and creators.

scenes.label: "AQUA INTERFACE"
scenes.script_text: When Jobs and his software engineers designed Mac OS X, they created the Aqua interface.

scenes.label: "BUTTONS YOU WANT TO LICK"
scenes.script_text: Jobs boasted to reporters: "We made the buttons on the screen look so good you'll want to lick them."

scenes.label: "RETAIL WILL FAIL"
scenes.script_text: In 2001, every retail expert told Jobs that building brick-and-mortar stores would be an expensive suicide mission.

scenes.label: "CONVENTIONAL WISDOM"
scenes.script_text: Gateway was closing its stores. Dell was selling exclusively online. Conventional wisdom said physical retail was dead.

scenes.label: "THE SECRET WAREHOUSE PROTOTYPE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs hired Mickey Drexler from Gap and built a secret prototype store inside an empty warehouse in Cupertino.

scenes.label: "FLORENTINE SANDSTONE FLOORS"
scenes.script_text: He insisted on genuine Italian pietra serena sandstone for the floors, quarried from a family-owned hillside in Florence.

scenes.label: "THE PATENTED GLASS STAIRCASE"
scenes.script_text: He patented the iconic spiral glass staircases, testing each floating glass tread to hold the weight of an elephant.

scenes.label: "THE GENIUS BAR"
scenes.script_text: The Genius Bar replaced traditional cash registers with friendly experts who fixed problems for free.

scenes.label: "$5,500 PER SQUARE FOOT"
scenes.script_text: Apple Stores became the most profitable retail spaces per square foot in the history of global commerce.

scenes.label: "SCRATCHED PLASTIC"
scenes.script_text: Six months before the iPhone launched, Steve Jobs made a furious discovery during testing.

scenes.label: "THE SCRATCH CRISIS"
scenes.script_text: He carried the prototype in his pocket with his car keys. The plastic screen was completely covered in scratches.

scenes.label: "IT MUST BE GLASS"
scenes.script_text: "I won't sell a product that gets scratched," Jobs raged. "I want a glass screen. And I want it perfect in six months."

scenes.label: "WENDELL WEEKS & GORILLA GLASS"
scenes.script_text: He called Wendell Weeks, the CEO of Corning Glass, who had an experimental glass recipe invented in the 1960s called 'Gorilla Glass.'

scenes.label: "THE FINAL SHADOW"
scenes.script_text: Behind the triumph, Steve Jobs was dying.

scenes.label: "THE PRIVATE FIGHT"
scenes.script_text: He had battled pancreatic cancer for eight grueling years.

scenes.label: "PASSING THE REINS"
scenes.script_text: In August 2011, knowing the end was near, Jobs resigned as CEO and handed the reins to his COO: Tim Cook.

scenes.label: "THE MASTER OF LOGISTICS"
scenes.script_text: Cook was an Alabama-born supply chain savant. Low-key, methodical, disciplined, and utterly unpretentious.

scenes.label: "THE LAST ADVICE"
scenes.script_text: Jobs's final advice to Cook was simple: 'Never ask what I would do. Just do what's right.'

scenes.label: "OCTOBER 5, 2011"
scenes.script_text: On October 5, 2011, Steve Jobs passed away at his home in Palo Alto at age fifty-six.

scenes.label: "THE GLOBAL SHRINES"
scenes.script_text: Across the globe, Apple retail stores became spontaneous shrines.

scenes.label: "THANK YOU, STEVE"
scenes.script_text: Mourners left real apples with bite marks taken out of them on the sidewalks.

scenes.label: "THE SKEPTICS"
scenes.script_text: Wall Street predicted Apple's doom. 'Without Jobs's creative genius,' critics wrote, 'Apple will fade.'

scenes.label: "WRONG AGAIN"
scenes.script_text: They were catastrophically wrong.

scenes.label: "THE INDUSTRIAL ENGINE"
scenes.script_text: Tim Cook did not try to be a rockstar visionary. He turned Apple into the most efficient manufacturing engine on earth.

scenes.label: "OUTSELLING SWITZERLAND"
scenes.script_text: He launched the Apple Watch, dominating the entire luxury timepiece industry.

scenes.label: "AIRPODS EMPIRE"
scenes.script_text: He launched AirPods, which by themselves make more revenue than most Fortune 500 corporations.

scenes.label: "APPLE SILICON"
scenes.script_text: He built Apple Silicon—the M1 and M-series chips—blowing Intel's processors out of the water.

scenes.label: "ONE TRILLION (2018)"
scenes.script_text: In August 2018, Apple became the first public American company in history to reach a one-trillion-dollar valuation.

scenes.label: "TWO TRILLION... THREE TRILLION"
scenes.script_text: Two years later, it hit two trillion. Then, three trillion.

scenes.label: "THE WEALTH MACHINE"
scenes.script_text: Under Tim Cook, Apple created more shareholder wealth than any corporate entity in human history.

scenes.label: "THE MORAL RECKONING"
scenes.script_text: Yet with ungodly scale came an unavoidable moral reckoning.

scenes.label: "IPHONE CITY: ZHENGZHOU"
scenes.script_text: In Zhengzhou, China—known as 'iPhone City'—over two hundred thousand factory workers assemble devices on grueling twelve-hour shifts.

scenes.label: "THE NETS"
scenes.script_text: Anti-suicide nets had to be strung along factory dormitories to catch exhausted workers.

scenes.label: "THE 30% APP TAX WAR"
scenes.script_text: Developers sued Apple over the thirty percent App Store 'tax,' comparing the walled garden to a feudal monopoly.

scenes.label: "USB-C MANDATE"
scenes.script_text: The European Union forced Apple to abandon its proprietary Lightning cable in favor of universal USB-C.

scenes.label: "ANTITRUST SCRUTINY"
scenes.script_text: Governments around the world launched antitrust probes, accusing Apple of suffocating competition and locking users in digital handcuffs.

scenes.label: "THE SILENT DINNER"
scenes.script_text: And millions of parents began noticing that their children couldn't look away from the little glowing glass rectangles.

scenes.label: "THE GOLDEN CAGE"
scenes.script_text: The company that promised to free humans from the totalitarian machine in 1984 had built its own inescapable digital cage.

scenes.label: "COMFORTABLE CAPTIVITY"
scenes.script_text: It was comfortable. It was beautiful. And nobody wanted to escape.

scenes.label: "THE GARAGE MEMORY"
scenes.script_text: In 1976, two broke kids in a drafty garage started building circuit boards because they thought technology should belong to the individual.

scenes.label: "ONE BILLION HEARTS"
scenes.script_text: Today, their creation governs the communications, finances, entertainment, and memories of over a billion human beings.

scenes.label: "BICYCLE FOR THE MIND"
scenes.script_text: They gave humanity a bicycle for the mind.

scenes.label: "WHO RIDES WHOM?"
scenes.script_text: The only question left is who is really riding whom.

scenes.label: "CRIST DRIVE TO APPLE PARK"
scenes.script_text: From an unpainted garage in Los Altos to a three-trillion-dollar glass empire.

scenes.label: "BUILT WITH US"
scenes.script_text: Thank you for building this story with us.

scenes.label: "SUBSCRIBE & LIKE"
scenes.script_text: If you felt the spark of this story, hit like and subscribe for the complete history of more empires, one founder at a time.

scenes.label: "TELL US IN THE COMMENTS"
scenes.script_text: And tell us in the comments below: what was the very first Apple product you ever held in your hands? The II, the iPod, or the iPhone?

scenes.label: "SEE YOU AT THE NEXT BUILD"
scenes.script_text: See you at the next build.

scenes.label: "IDLE OVENS"
scenes.script_text: Corning had never manufactured Gorilla Glass in mass quantities. Weeks said it would take years to scale.

scenes.label: "SIX MONTHS TO RE-TOOL"
scenes.script_text: Jobs replied: "Don't be afraid. You can do this. Get your mind around it." Within six months, Corning converted an entire factory.

scenes.label: "UNBREAKABLE GLASS"
scenes.script_text: When the first iPhone shipped on June 29, 2007, it had a flawless, diamond-hard Gorilla Glass display.

scenes.label: "THE SUPPLY CHAIN ARCHITECT"
scenes.script_text: When Tim Cook took over, he quietly revolutionized corporate operations.

scenes.label: "ZERO INVENTORY DELAY"
scenes.script_text: Cook eliminated Apple's owned warehouses, slashing inventory holding time from months to just hours.

scenes.label: "THE 48-HOUR PIPELINE"
scenes.script_text: If a computer part sat on a shelf for three days, Cook considered it a criminal waste of capital.

scenes.label: "THE TITANIUM CARD"
scenes.script_text: In 2019, Apple introduced the Apple Card, crafted out of laser-etched pure titanium.

scenes.label: "THE VISION PRO"
scenes.script_text: In 2023, Apple unveiled the Vision Pro, attempting to replace flat screens with spatial computing.

scenes.label: "THE 50-YEAR EVOLUTION"
scenes.script_text: From room-sized mainframe computers to personal computers, to pocket screens, to computers strapped directly to human faces.

scenes.label: "CLOSER TO CONSCIOUSNESS"
scenes.script_text: The trajectory has always been the same: moving the digital world closer and closer to human consciousness.

scenes.label: "A BICYCLE FOR THE MIND"
scenes.script_text: Steve Jobs once said that computers were the equivalent of a bicycle for our minds.

scenes.label: "INTO THE STRATOSPHERE"
scenes.script_text: Fifty years later, that bicycle has carried Apple into the stratosphere of human civilization.

scenes.label: "A DENT IN THE UNIVERSE"
scenes.script_text: A company built by outcasts, pirates, and dreamers who believed they could dent the universe.

scenes.label: "THE DENT REMAINS"
scenes.script_text: And against every rational probability in corporate history, they did.
